ch01.anchor: Tenshō 10
ch01.note: 1582 by the Western calendar (printed folio 6). The Tenshō era ran 1573-1592; this particular year would see the deaths of both Nobunaga and the Takeda house, and, at its very end for the story's purposes, the turning of the whole political order.

ch01.anchor: his great castle at Azuchi
ch01.note: Azuchi Castle, on the shore of Lake Biwa, was Nobunaga's magnificent new seat, its keep famous for its gilded and painted interior. It was burned within days of his death.

ch01.anchor: Ōhara, to Daigo, to Arashiyama
ch01.note: Noted cherry-blossom and scenic spots on the outskirts of Kyoto, to the north, southeast, and west of the city respectively.

ch01.anchor: The bell for the Angelus
ch01.note: The Angelus is a Catholic devotion said at morning, noon, and evening, called to by a bell. That such a bell should ring over Kyoto at all is the measure of how far the mission had come in a few years.

ch01.anchor: their orasho
ch01.note: Orasho (from Latin oratio, prayer) was the Japanese Christians' word for their set prayers, many memorized in Latin or Portuguese and handed down by rote long after the missionaries were gone.

ch01.anchor: O saving Victim, who openest the gate of Heaven
ch01.note: The prayer the girls recite is a Japanese rendering of the Latin eucharistic hymn O Salutaris Hostia (“O saving Victim, opening wide the gate of heaven; our foes press hard on every side, thine aid supply, thy strength bestow”), by Thomas Aquinas. The correspondence is exact, line for line.

ch01.anchor: the rosary-beads called contas
ch01.note: Contas (Portuguese, prayer-beads) and cruz (cross) are among the many Portuguese loanwords the mission left in Japanese; the beads and crosses sold at the gate were devotional goods for converts.

ch01.anchor: the garça, the grace, of Deus
ch01.note: Garça renders Portuguese graça, grace. Such Portuguese religious terms were absorbed wholesale, since no Buddhist or Shinto word carried the meaning.

ch01.anchor: Padre Organtino
ch01.note: Gnecchi-Soldo Organtino (1533-1609), an Italian Jesuit who reached Japan in 1570 and spent decades in and around Kyoto. He was known for an unusual warmth toward the Japanese and their culture. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: the Nanban-ji: the temple of the southern barbarians
ch01.note: The Jesuit church in Kyoto, dedicated to Our Lady of the Assumption and completed about 1576. Nanban (“southern barbarian”) was the ordinary Japanese term for the Portuguese and Spanish, who reached Japan by the southern sea routes. The building was destroyed after the anti-Christian edicts of the following decade.

ch01.anchor: Francisco Xavier
ch01.note: St Francis Xavier (1506-1552), the Jesuit co-founder who opened the Japan mission, landing at Kagoshima on 15 August 1549. That the day was the Feast of the Assumption is the reason given here for the church's dedication. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: Murai Sadakatsu himself, the shoshidai of Kyoto
ch01.note: Murai Sadakatsu (d. 1582) was Nobunaga's shoshidai, his military governor of the capital. That even he contributed to the church shows how far Nobunaga's favor extended to the mission. He would die defending Nobunaga's son at the fall of Nijo the same year.

ch01.anchor: Like the Ikkō sect before it
ch01.note: The Ikko-shu, a militant strand of the Jodo Shinshu (True Pure Land) school, had built peasant leagues (ikki) powerful enough to war with the warlords for a decade; Nobunaga crushed them at terrible cost. The novel's point is that both movements drew their strength from the poor.

ch01.anchor: chant the nenbutsu
ch01.note: The nenbutsu is the invocation “Namu Amida Butsu” (“Hail Amida Buddha”), whose repetition, in Pure Land teaching, assures rebirth in the Buddha's paradise.

ch01.anchor: set out by Padre Gaspar Coelho
ch01.note: Gaspar Coelho (c. 1531-1590), Portuguese Jesuit and vice-provincial of the Japan mission. The exchange over polygamy is drawn from the Jesuit accounts; whether Hideyoshi spoke quite these words is uncorroborated, but his later reversal against the mission is history.

ch01.anchor: told the irmão
ch01.note: Irmão (Portuguese, “brother”) was a Jesuit lay brother or catechist, ranking below the padre (Japanese bateren). Many irmãos in Japan were themselves Japanese.

ch01.anchor: the Raichō Jikki
ch01.note: “A True Record of the Coming to Court,” an old account the novel cites for this startled Japanese description of a European's looks. The grotesque catalogue (yellow eyes, bear's claws, mouse-colored hair) records how alien the first Europeans appeared.

ch01.anchor: retainers of Takayama Ukon
ch01.note: Takayama Ukon (1552-1615), the most famous of the Christian daimyo, who chose exile over apostasy and died in Manila. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: Luís Fróis
ch01.note: Luis Frois (1532-1597), Portuguese Jesuit and the mission's great chronicler; his Historia de Japam is a chief source for the events and personalities of these very years.

ch01.anchor: the Compendium of the Great Deeds of Pope Gregory XIII
ch01.note: Gregory XIII (pope 1572-1585) received the Tensho embassy of Japanese Christian boys in 1585; a commemorative volume of his pontificate carried an imagined view of the Azuchi seminary, which the novel here corrects. The point — that a European artist drew a stone cathedral where a tile-roofed Japanese building stood — is well taken.

ch01.anchor: Jerome Itō, son of Itō Yoshimasu, the daimyō of Hyūga
ch01.note: Of the Christian Ito house of Hyuga (in southern Kyushu); the family gave the Tensho embassy its leader, Ito Mancio. “Jerome” (Geronimo) is his Christian name. A Japanese boy playing a keyboard for Nobunaga captures the novelty of the moment.

ch01.anchor: Vilela's report calls those peasants
ch01.note: Gaspar Vilela (c. 1526-1572), Portuguese Jesuit, one of the first to work in Kyoto. The bitter phrase about peasants as “slaves” of samurai and priests reflects both the Jesuits' observation and the author's own sympathies.

ch01.anchor: First seize the soul, and then the country.
ch01.note: Here the author, Murayama — a lifelong man of the political left — reads the mission through the lens of European colonialism, casting even the sincere missionaries as unwitting agents of conquest. The judgment is his interpretation, offered as such; the sincerity and self-sacrifice of men like Organtino he does not deny.

ch01.anchor: made for their roosts on Mount Hiei
ch01.note: Mount Hiei, northeast of Kyoto, was the seat of the great Tendai monastery Enryaku-ji, which Nobunaga had stormed and burned to the ground in 1571, massacring its monks — a deliberate contrast here with the Christian church in the city below.

ch01.anchor: This was Honnō-ji itself, the head temple of the Hokke sect
ch01.note: Honno-ji, a temple of the Hokke-shu (Nichiren Buddhism). The “great turn” three months off is the Honno-ji Incident of the 2nd of the sixth month, 1582, when Akechi Mitsuhide turned his army against his lord and Nobunaga died in the burning temple. The foreshadowing here is the hinge of the whole book.

ch01.anchor: the battle of Nagashino
ch01.note: At Nagashino (1575) the combined Oda and Tokugawa armies, using massed arquebus fire from behind palisades, destroyed the Takeda cavalry — the disaster from which the Takeda never recovered. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: took his own life, together with his wife and his kin
ch01.note: Katsuyori's suicide at Tenmokuzan on the 11th of the third month, 1582, ended the Takeda house. The details — the defections, the handful of men left — follow the standard accounts. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: Quench the mind, and the very fire is cool
ch01.note: The burning of Erin-ji, where the abbot Kaisen had sheltered Nobunaga's enemies, is historical (1582). Kaisen's death-verse — in full, “There is no need of mountains and streams for quiet meditation; quench the mind, and even fire is cool” — became one of the most famous lines in Japanese Zen. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: a great comet threw the people of Kyoto into alarm
ch01.note: A bright comet was in fact recorded over Japan in the summer of 1582 and noted in several court diaries as an evil omen; the great events that followed within weeks fixed it in memory. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: The visitador, the inspector Valignano
ch01.note: Alessandro Valignano (1539–1606), the Jesuit Visitor to the East Indies, whose inspection tours shaped the whole Japan mission; it was he who organized the seminaries and, in 1582, sent the four Christian boys of the Tensho embassy to Europe. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: a black man he had carried with him from Africa
ch01.note: This is the man history knows as Yasuke, an African whom Valignano brought to Japan and presented to Nobunaga in 1581. Nobunaga took him into his service — making him, by some accounts, the first foreigner to be granted the standing of a samurai. The scene of Nobunaga scrubbing at his skin, and his survival of Honnō-ji (Mitsuhide spared him and gave him up to the Jesuits), both come from the contemporary Jesuit letters. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: the Momochi fort
ch01.note: Momochi — the name of Momochi Sandayu (also called Tamba), one of the great chieftains of the Iga ninja. Tamo is thus a survivor of the Tensho Iga War of 1581, in which Nobunaga's armies overran the self-governing ninja communities of Iga and put their strongholds to fire and sword. It is the hidden hinge of her whole story, and it binds her to the shinobi world that is the novel's true subject.

ch01.anchor: Prince Sanehito, son of the Retired Emperor Ōgimachi
ch01.note: Emperor Ogimachi (r. 1557–1586) and his son and heir-apparent, Prince Sanehito. The Nijo Palace where Nobutada made his stand adjoined the imperial quarter, and the prince had to be hurried to safety before the fighting closed in — a measure of how near the catastrophe came to the throne itself. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: The Minister of the Right
ch01.note: Court ranks: Nobunaga held the office of Udaijin, Minister of the Right; his son Nobutada was a Sanmi-chujo, a Middle Captain of the Third Rank. The attackers use the formal titles even as they call for the men's deaths.

ch01.anchor: the Seta Bridge
ch01.note: The Seta no Karahashi, at the outflow of Lake Biwa, was the strategic gateway to Azuchi and the east; controlling or cutting it governed any advance on Nobunaga's capital. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: Padre Francisco Fróis
ch01.note: The mission's great chronicler is usually named Luis Frois; the given name here differs, and the novel may be conflating him with, or naming, another Jesuit at the Azuchi seminary. Rendered as printed.

ch01.anchor: the two armies joined battle at Yamazaki
ch01.note: The battle of Yamazaki, on the 13th of the sixth month, 1582, eleven days after Honnō-ji. Hideyoshi's forced march back from the Chugoku front (the famous “Great Return”), bought by a hurried peace with the Mori and Shimizu Muneharu's ritual suicide, caught Mitsuhide before he could consolidate. Mitsuhide's rule had lasted scarcely eleven days — the proverbial “three-day reign” — and his death near Ogurusu at the hands of peasant looters left the field, and Nobunaga's inheritance, to Hideyoshi. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: at Ichijōdani in Echizen
ch01.note: Ichijodani, the castle-town of the Asakura clan in Echizen (modern Fukui), was overrun and burned by Nobunaga in 1573 when he destroyed the Asakura. Tamo is thus a survivor of two of Nobunaga's exterminations, a decade apart — Ichijodani and Iga — which is why his rotting head holds her as it does. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: the famous Tarao Crossing of Tokugawa Ieyasu
ch01.note: When Nobunaga died, Ieyasu was deep in hostile country near Sakai with a tiny escort, and had to race home to Mikawa across the mountains of Iga and Koga, guided and guarded by local ninja under Hattori Hanzo. The “Tarao crossing” (also called the Iga crossing) became legend, and the debt Ieyasu owed the shinobi that day is the traditional root of the ninja's long service to the Tokugawa. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: In the generation of Hanzō's father
ch01.note: Hattori Hanzo — here Hattori Masanari (1542–1596), “Hanzo the Devil,” the most famous ninja captain in Japanese memory, who led Ieyasu's Iga men and later commanded a corps of them in Edo. A gate of Edo Castle still bears his name (Hanzomon). Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: rose to be shinobi of the middle rank
ch01.note: The shinobi were graded in three ranks: jonin (upper), the masters who directed operations and dealt with employers; chunin (middle), the field commanders; and genin (lower), the agents who did the actual work. The Chigachi/Hattori line stood in the middle tier.

ch01.anchor: Ishikawa Goemon
ch01.note: The novel's hero, here glimpsed only as a yardstick for another man's face. Ishikawa Goemon is the great outlaw of Japanese legend — thief, shinobi, and folk avenger — whose death by boiling in an iron cauldron (the subtitle's “Goemon boiled in the cauldron”) is fixed in popular memory. History records the execution; almost everything else about him is legend, which the novel takes as its material.

ch01.anchor: five shaku eight sun
ch01.note: About 176 centimetres — tall for the period. Traditional units used through the book: the shaku is roughly 30 cm and the sun a tenth of it (~3 cm); a chō is about 109 metres and a ri about 3.9 kilometres; a ryō is a gold coin, the standard large unit of money.

ch01.anchor: the battle of Dan-no-ura
ch01.note: The sea-battle of 1185 that ended the Genpei War with the annihilation of the Taira (Heike) clan; Taira no Tomomori, a Taira commander, died there. Claiming descent from a Heike survivor was a common pedigree for provincial warrior houses.

ch01.anchor: Honda Tadakatsu
ch01.note: Honda Tadakatsu (1548–1610), one of the “Four Guardian Kings” of the Tokugawa, celebrated as a warrior who came through countless battles without a wound.

ch01.anchor: the great Kyoto merchant Chaya Shirōjirō
ch01.note: Chaya Shirojiro (Kiyonobu), a Kyoto merchant close to Ieyasu; by tradition it was his money, scattered along the way, that bought the peasants' help and safe passage on the Tarao crossing. His house prospered mightily under the Tokugawa afterward. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: the fifty-three houses of Kōga
ch01.note: Koga, the district just north of Iga, was the other great homeland of the shinobi; its warrior families — traditionally reckoned fifty-three — formed a self-governing league much like Iga's, and the two are always named together. Their local power is exactly what made them worth cultivating for a fugitive lord.

ch01.anchor: caught up in the Ōnin War
ch01.note: The Onin War (1467–1477), a struggle over the Ashikaga shogunal succession that wrecked Kyoto and broke central authority, is the conventional opening of the Sengoku (“Warring States”) age — the century of chaos in which this whole novel is set. Ashikaga Yoshimi and the shogun Yoshimasa were the rival claimants' figures at its heart.

ch01.anchor: Fujibayashi Nagato-no-kami or a Momochi Sandayū
ch01.note: The two legendary jonin masters of Iga, the shadowy chiefs who directed the ninja from windowless keeps. Momochi Sandayu is of the same Momochi house whose mountain fort was the scene of Tamo's maiming; the name threads her story quietly into the ninja world the novel is now opening up. Both are half-legend: some traditions even make them one man under two names.

ch01.anchor: twenty-two kan
ch01.note: The kan is a unit of weight of about 3.75 kilograms, so the boy weighs some 82 kg and Etegi about 154 kg — enormous figures, and the joke of the scene: two ninja who are anything but light on their feet.

ch01.anchor: at the siege of Ishiyama
ch01.note: The ten-year war (1570–1580) in which the Ishiyama Hongan-ji, headquarters of the Ikko league at Osaka, held out against Nobunaga — the longest and bitterest of his struggles with the militant Pure Land peasantry. Karasumaru, orphaned son of an Ikko commander, is a child of that world; the ninja and the Ikko leagues are two faces of the same resistance from below that the novel keeps in view.

ch01.anchor: There was no road open to her but to yield in silence.
ch01.note: The narrator's flat, unsparing statement of a woman's powerlessness in this world is the author writing as a modern man of the left: he neither excuses the custom nor lets the reader mistake it for romance. The same sympathy for those with no say in their fate runs under his treatment of peasants, ninja, and the poor throughout.

ch01.anchor: the Magari no Jin
ch01.note: The “Camp at Magari” (1487–1489), the campaign in which the ninth Ashikaga shogun, Yoshihisa, marched on the Rokkaku of Omi and bogged down; the Koga warriors who harried his camp with fire and night-raids first made the ninja famous, and the shogun himself died in the field. It is the traditional debut of the ninja on the stage of national history, which is why the novel pauses on it. Corroborated in outline; the marvels, as the text goes on to say, are later embroidery.

ch01.anchor: the model for the Special Higher Police
ch01.note: Here the author's own century breaks in. The Hanzo Gate (Hanzomon) of Edo Castle — and today a Tokyo subway line — is named for Hattori Hanzo; and Murayama, a man of the left who had himself been jailed and interrogated under the prewar thought-police, traces a deliberate line from the Tokugawa spy service Hanzo ran to the Tokko, the Special Higher Police that hounded dissidents in his own lifetime. It is one of the book's sharpest reminders that its author is writing history with a stake in the present.

ch01.anchor: forced to take his own life by his own father, Ieyasu
ch01.note: The death of Matsudaira (Tokugawa) Nobuyasu in 1579 is historical, and one of the darkest episodes of Ieyasu's rise: under pressure from Nobunaga — and on charges pressed by his own wife, Nobunaga's daughter — Ieyasu had his heir put to death and his wife, the Lady Tsukiyama, killed. Historians still debate how far Nobunaga compelled it and how far Ieyasu chose it; the novel gives the traditional account, in which Ieyasu bows to a power he cannot yet defy. Corroborated in outline.

ch01.anchor: and the second was Hattori Hanzō
ch01.note: In seppuku, the kaishaku or second stood ready to behead the man the instant he had cut himself, cutting short the agony; to be asked was an honor and a heavy trust. That Hanzo — a hardened killer — could not bring the blade down on his young lord is the human core of the scene, and the reason he raised a temple for him afterward.

ch01.anchor: the peasants of Etchū and Kaga governed their own country themselves
ch01.note: This is the heart of the author's sympathies. The Ikko (True Pure Land) leagues built, for a time, something like peasant self-rule: Kaga was famously called “the province held by the peasants,” governed for nearly a century by the league in defiance of the warrior lords, until Nobunaga broke it. Koichi's plain praise of Karasumaru's father — a leader who lowered the peasants' taxes and let no samurai touch them — frames the Ikko resistance, like the ninja, as a revolt of the powerless, which is how Murayama reads his whole century.

ch01.anchor: a wicked Iga ninja named Kashii
ch01.note: The same Kashii who, at the Momochi fort, burned to death shielding Tamo, and whom she mourns. Here, through a child's memory, we learn he was also the ninja who took the head of Karasumaru's father and brought Toyama Castle down. The novel quietly knots its strangers together: the man one survivor loves is the man another's tragedy turns on.

ch01.anchor: will surely have become a socialist country
ch01.note: The author steps bodily into his own book — naming his real grandson and nephew — and lets slip a flat confidence that Japan will be socialist within a generation. Written around 1962, at the high tide of the postwar Japanese left, the prediction dates the book's optimism as sharply as any footnote could, and marks openly the political faith through which Murayama tells this sixteenth-century story.

ch01.anchor: Mr. Hatsumi Masaaki
ch01.note: Here the author cites a living authority: Masaaki Hatsumi (b. 1931), the modern grandmaster who claims the headship of the Togakure-ryu school of ninjutsu and whose demonstrations and writings did much to spread ninja lore in the twentieth century. Murayama's point is that the physical feats in his story are not fantasy but attested tradition, handed down through a real, named lineage.

ch01.anchor: I am a woman ninja!
ch01.note: The kunoichi — the woman of the shinobi — is the thread being drawn taut here. Hatsuko's declaration, and Tamo's girlhood skill glimpsed a page earlier, set the two women's fates on the same axis; and the author, breaking in with the memory of his own widowed, browbeaten mother, makes plain that he means the female ninja as a figure of a woman seizing power in a world built to deny her any. The claim — that she will not sell the art but use it for herself — is the book's quiet manifesto.

ch01.anchor: a great many local magnates and land-samurai sprang up
ch01.note: The dogo (local magnates) and jizamurai (land-holding warrior-farmers) were the backbone of Iga and Koga society: not lords with fiefs granted from above, but self-made men of the land who banded into leagues to govern themselves. The ninja were drawn from exactly this class, which is why the author roots their character in the soil and rivers of the two provinces — the richer land of Koga breeding one kind of man, the poor mountains of Iga another.

ch01.anchor: the twenty-two volumes of the Bansenshūkai
ch01.note: The Bansenshukai (“Sea of Ten Thousand Rivers Gathered,” 1676) is the great surviving encyclopedia of ninjutsu, and the Shoninki (1681) another key manual; both are real, and the researchers the author names — Okuse Heishichiro, Yamaguchi Masayuki — are real scholars of the subject. Murayama is showing his work: for all the novel's play, its ninja lore is drawn from documents a reader can go and check. His point about the manuals is a sharp one — that a secret art gets written down only once it is no longer a living, dangerous craft.

ch01.anchor: the Mochizuki house that stands to this day
ch01.note: Real places, both. The Mochizuki residence at Koka (Ryuhoshi) survives as the “Koka Ninja House,” a farmhouse honeycombed with trapdoors, hidden ladders and escape hatches, open to visitors; and the “Nijo house” is the Nijo Jinya in Kyoto, a merchant's mansion built with the same defensive trickery. That the author has walked through them, and that a Mochizuki descendant now sells patent medicine, collapses the four centuries between his story and his reader.

ch01.anchor: Irmão Lourenço
ch01.note: Lourenco Ryosai (c.1526–1592) is one of the tenderest true figures in the whole Japanese mission: a blind, half-sighted biwa hoshi — a wandering lute-priest — from Hizen, converted by Xavier at Yamaguchi around 1551, who became the first Japanese admitted as a Jesuit brother and, despite his blindness, one of the mission's most persuasive preachers. Everything the novel gives him here — the birth in Hizen, the begging with the biwa, the meeting with Xavier at Yamaguchi — is drawn from the record. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: the Dutch pirates
ch01.note: The gunpowder trade the confessing merchant describes — sulfur out, muskets and shot in, off the coast of Saiga (Saika) in Kishu, home of the great gunner-league — is true to the period; the arms trade made men like this rich and armed every warlord in Japan. “Dutch,” though, is a slip or a loose usage: in 1582 the sea-traders and gun-sellers were the Portuguese and Spanish (the Nanban); the Dutch did not reach Japan until about 1600. Rendered as printed.

ch01.anchor: the novel The Stealthy Ones came to its close
ch01.note: The book breaks its own frame at the end. This volume — Shinobi no Mono: Goemon Boiled in the Cauldron — continues Murayama's long Goemon saga, and the whole of this first chapter has been a bridge: setting the stage of 1582 (Honno-ji, the fall of the Takeda, the ninja's turn to the Tokugawa, the Christian mission) before the narrator turns time back a year to rejoin his hero. The “new waves of history” he names are the chapter's own title, and Goemon's story proper begins with the next.

ch02.note: The end of 1581. Chapter 1 opened in the spring of Tenshō 10 (1582); the narrator has now, as he promised there, turned the clock back about a year to rejoin Goemon. The whole of this chapter therefore runs up to, and through, the events of the first chapter from the other side. (Printed folio 70.)

Chinu (Chinu no umi) is the old poetic name for the stretch of sea off Sakai and Izumi, the eastern reach of what is now Osaka Bay. It is named again and again in the ancient poetry, which is the point of the lines that follow. (Printed folio 72.)

ch02.anchor: this poem stands in the Man'yōshū
ch02.note: The Man’yōshū (“Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves,” compiled in the eighth century) is Japan’s oldest anthology of verse. The poem — a lover soaked to the sleeve gathering shells on the Chinu shore — is one of its anonymous pieces; the narrator’s joke is that an unlettered thief like Goemon repeats its very gesture without any notion that a classical poem has said it first. (Printed folio 73.)

Nabari lies in the north of Iga province. The cover story is quietly ironic: to hide that he is an Iga shinobi, Goemon invents a false self who is nonetheless from Iga, planting “Tahei” a short ride from his real birthplace at Ishikawa. (Printed folio 73.)

The Ten Commandments as the Jesuits taught them in Japan; the “rules for the wiping-out of sin” are the examination of conscience made before confession. The numbering follows the Catholic decalogue — the sixth against adultery, the ninth against coveting another man’s wife — and the searching questions about sins of desire are drawn straight from the confessors’ manuals of the mission. (Printed folio 71.)

Nanzen-ji is a great Zen monastery in eastern Kyoto; its towering two-storey gate (the Sanmon) is bound up with the Goemon legend. In the famous kabuki Sanmon Gosan no Kiri (1778) the outlaw Goemon lounges atop this very gate and cries, at the spring view, “What a prospect! What a prospect!” The novel nods to that legend by lodging its Goemon in the gate-tower among the temple’s dry-lacquer Buddhas. (Printed folio 75.)

Kariteimo (Sanskrit Hārītī), popularly Kishimojin. By the legend she was an ogress who devoured other people’s children until the Buddha hid one of her own thousand children to teach her a mother’s grief; converted, she became the guardian of childbirth and of infants, and is shown holding a pomegranate. She is especially honored in Nichiren Buddhism. (Printed folio 76.)

ch02.anchor: a Santa Maria holding the child Jezus Kirishito
ch02.note: A Christian image made in Buddhist form. The Christian daimyō Takayama Ukon (see chapter 1) held Takatsuki from 1573 and raised churches there; a Madonna-and-Child carved by a Japanese Buddhist sculptor would sit at the very root of the later “Maria Kannon,” the disguised Marian images by which hidden Christians kept their faith through the persecution. Goemon, taking it for a Kishimojin, sees only that its face is Maki’s. (Printed folio 77.)

One of the most famous of the Sakai merchant princes, better remembered as Ruson (Luzon) Sukezaemon. As the text goes on to say, he sailed to Luzon in the Spanish Philippines and came home laden with treasure; he later fell foul of Hideyoshi, who coveted his imported wares, and by tradition fled Japan for the southern seas. Much of his story is half legend. (Printed folio 77.)

ch02.anchor: the History of the Western Religion in Japan
ch02.note: Nihon Seikyō-shi, a later Japanese history of the Christian mission drawing on the Jesuit letters and chronicles. Here it and Padre Gaspar Vilela’s 1562 letter (Vilela: see chapter 1) are cited as real documentary evidence for how strongly Sakai was fortified. (Printed folio 78.)

Sakai governed itself, in this age, through a council of thirty-six wealthy townsmen, the egōshū, the ten strongest of whom (the naya-shū, the “warehouse men”) held the real power. The Jesuit Frois likened the free merchant city to Venice. That autonomy ended when Nobunaga brought Sakai under a magistrate of his own. (Printed folio 78.)

ch02.anchor: Kuki Yoshitaka built ten iron ships
ch02.note: Kuki Yoshitaka was Nobunaga’s admiral. In 1578 he built a squadron of great iron-plated warships and with them smashed the Mōri navy at the mouth of the Kizu River, cutting off the sea route by which the Mōri had been resupplying the Ishiyama Hongan-ji. Most accounts number the ironclads at six or seven rather than the ten the novel gives. (Printed folio 79.)

The sotetsu (sago palm, or cycad) of the Myōkoku-ji is the subject of a well-loved Sakai legend, told here in full: Nobunaga coveted the great old plant and had it moved to Azuchi, whereupon it wailed each night to be taken home, until he gave up and returned it. The cycad is not native to Japan; it was carried up from the south, which is why Goemon feels in it a homesickness from far away. (Printed folio 80.)

The jō is ten shaku, roughly three metres (for the smaller units of length see chapter 1). The tree thus stood something over three and a half metres, and better than five around at the root. (Printed folio 81.)

This ninja explanation of Takeda Shingen’s death belongs to the world of the earlier novel, not to the record. Shingen died in 1573 during the withdrawal from Noda castle; the histories put it down to illness, though one old tradition has it he was hit by a sniper’s ball at the siege. The tale of an Iga poisoner is the story’s own. (Printed folio 87.)

The shichihōde, the “seven ways out,” were the seven stock disguises of the Iga and Kōga shinobi for travel in hostile provinces: priest, mountain ascetic, flute-playing komusō, street conjuror, sarugaku player, merchant, and plain townsman. The point, as the ferryman anecdote makes plain, was not costume but total impersonation. (Printed folio 86.)

A koku was reckoned as the rice a man eats in a year (about 180 litres), and a warrior’s stipend was measured in it. Thirty koku with three men’s keep is a very small holding — set beside the five hundred thousand koku of a great lord like Mitsuhide, later in the chapter, it marks Goemon’s deliberately humble footing in the Tokugawa house. (Printed folio 89.)

ch02.anchor: swift as the wind, still as the forest
ch02.note: The motto of Takeda Shingen’s war-banner, the celebrated Fūrinkazan (“Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain”), taken from Sun Tzu: swift as wind, silent as forest, fierce as fire, unshakable as mountain. Tradition holds the characters were brushed by Kaisen, the abbot of Erin-ji, whose burning by Nobunaga is the scene here (Kaisen and Erin-ji: see chapter 1). (Printed folio 94.)

The old war-tales made much of Nobunaga humiliating Akechi Mitsuhide — the beating before the gate of Erin-ji, the stripping of the banquet office at Azuchi — and treated these slights as the spur to the Honnō-ji revolt three weeks later. Modern historians read most of it as later embroidery and leave Mitsuhide’s true motive an open question; the novel adopts the traditional, dramatic account, and adds a hidden hand behind it. (Printed folio 96.)

ch02.anchor: Momochi Sandayū and Fujibayashi Nagato-no-kami had been one and the same man
ch02.note: The notion that Iga’s two legendary chief shinobi were a single man wearing two names comes out of the earlier novel (on the pair, see chapter 1). Goemon guards the secret because he alone is placed to know it, and because it cannot, he thinks, be disproved. (Printed folio 127.)

Nobunaga’s best-loved page and, by tradition, his boy-lover; such bonds (nanshoku) between a lord and a youth were an accepted part of samurai life. Ranmaru and his younger brothers Bōmaru and Rikimaru all died at his side at the Honnō-ji. He was about eighteen. (Printed folio 96.)

ch02.anchor: The enemy is at the Honnō-ji.
ch02.note: The most famous line of the whole affair, put in Mitsuhide’s mouth as he turned his army from the Bitchū road toward Kyoto. It is almost certainly a later dramatist’s invention rather than a recorded utterance, but it has become the shorthand for the betrayal itself (on the Honnō-ji: see chapter 1). (Printed folio 106.)

ch02.anchor: At Mount Hiei you burned a thousand six hundred souls
ch02.note: Goemon’s indictment lists Nobunaga’s notorious slaughters: the burning of the Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei in 1571 (Mount Hiei: see chapter 1), and the massacre of the Ikkō leagues penned up at Nagashima in Ise in 1574, where tens of thousands were burned to death — figures vary widely, and the fourteen thousand given here is at the low end of the estimates. (Printed folio 110.)

ch02.anchor: the perils of the Iga crossing
ch02.note: Ieyasu’s flight home after the Honnō-ji Incident, over the mountains of Iga to his own country, guided by Hattori Hanzō’s Iga men — the celebrated “Iga crossing” (the same escape called the Tarao Crossing in chapter 1), long remembered as the tightest scrape of his life. (Printed folio 110.)

The Peanuts were Emi and Yumi Itō, identical-twin sisters and one of the most popular singing acts in the Japan of the early 1960s, when this novel was being written — and, to Western readers, the tiny twin fairies of the Mothra films. The author reaches into his own present for a resemblance no reader of his day could miss. (Printed folio 115.)

The author, Murayama Tomoyoshi (1901–1977) — avant-garde painter, playwright, and director of the proletarian theatre — was repeatedly tailed and jailed for his left-wing work in the 1930s. His running asides on detectives and their memory for faces, like the tirade earlier in the chapter, come straight out of that experience (compare the aside on the Special Higher Police in chapter 1). (Printed folio 86.)

En no Gyōja (En no Ozunu), the semi-legendary seventh-century ascetic revered as the founder of Shugendō, the mountain asceticism that the novel treats as the root of ninjutsu. The Peacock King (Kujaku Myōō) whose rite follows is a wisdom-king invoked in esoteric Shingon against poison and sickness and for long life. (Printed folio 129.)

ch02.anchor: Kōbō Daishi, founder of the Shingon sect
ch02.note: Kūkai (774–835), the great master of esoteric Buddhism. Believers hold that he did not die but sits in eternal meditation in the inner sanctuary (Oku-no-in) of Kōya-san, awaiting the future Buddha Maitreya — who is said to come five and a half billion years after Śākyamuni — and that the pilgrim who nears his tomb, chanting “Namu Daishi Henjō Kongō,” draws near a living presence. The narrator sets this beside the Christian hope of the Second Coming. (Printed folio 129.)

The author, a lifelong Marxist, quietly enlists his outlaw hero in his own creed: death is the end, the soul only a working of the body. The “us” is the tell — the whole long meditation on resurrection and deathlessness is the materialist author measuring the consolations of religion and finding them wanting, while granting how naturally the people of Goemon’s age lived inside them. (Printed folio 131.)

ch03.anchor: But that was the underside of it
ch03.note: The chapter's title and method, Omote to Ura: the visible official face of an event against its hidden workings. Here the narrator names it outright — Mitsuhide the arch-traitor on the surface, Hideyoshi's benefactor underneath — and the whole chapter works the two together, retelling the fall of Nobunaga and the rise of Hideyoshi from the chronicles and the kabuki stage (the surface) against Goemon and the ninja net (the underside). (Printed folio 152.)

ch03.anchor: The Shinsho Taikōki is a vast work
ch03.note: The Shinsho Taikōki (真書太閣記), a huge popular chronicle of Hideyoshi in twelve series and 360 volumes by Kurihara Ryūan (1794–1870). Written as history but shaped as entertainment, it makes an unclouded hero of Hideyoshi; the narrator quotes it through the chapter as the “surface” record, and picks it apart. (Printed folio 139.)

ch03.anchor: Lady Shizuka at the Horikawa night-attack
ch03.note: Two stock allusions the chronicle reaches for. Shizuka Gozen, the dancer and mistress of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, is by tradition the one who raised the alarm at the night raid on Yoshitsune’s Horikawa mansion; the “sister of Manabe no Rokurō-dayū” is another old-tale byword for a woman of warrior spirit. (Printed folio 140.)

ch03.anchor: Bakin's Satomi Hakkenden
ch03.note: Kyokutei Bakin’s Nansō Satomi Hakkenden (1814–1842), a vast epic novel of eight dog-warriors. The narrator sorts Edo fiction into the sharebon, light popular writing, and the yomihon, the ambitious literary novel to which the Hakkenden belongs; the Taikōki, he notes, was written not as either but as history. (Printed folio 141.)

ch03.anchor: a gift for the court of Enma
ch03.note: Enma (Sanskrit Yama), the king and judge of the dead who assigns the newly dead to their fate. To “make a man a gift for Enma’s court” is to kill him and send him to hell. (Printed folio 142.)

ch03.anchor: the Seven Bands of Musashi
ch03.note: The Musashi Shichitō, seven medieval warrior leagues of Musashi province (the Kantō plain around modern Tokyo); a byword for hardy provincial fighting men. (Printed folio 142.)

ch03.anchor: press in on it from one position after another
ch03.note: The narrator states his method, and the chapter’s theme, outright: he has now told the fall of Nobunaga three times over — from the side of the Christian mission (Chapter 1), from Goemon’s own living of it (Chapter 2), and now from the popular chronicle — on the principle that a truth shows itself only when it is approached from many sides at once. (Printed folio 143.)

ch03.anchor: Look up kamari in the Kōjirin
ch03.note: Kamari: a stealth-scout or skirmisher. The Kōjirin is a standard modern Japanese dictionary; the narrator’s habit of stopping to check a word in a reference book is part of his plain, materialist, show-your-working manner. (Printed folio 144.)

ch03.anchor: none other than Katō Toranosuke
ch03.note: Katō Kiyomasa (1562–1611), here under his boyhood name Toranosuke: one of Hideyoshi’s most celebrated captains, later a great daimyo of Higo and famed castle-builder. He appears twice in this chapter’s quoted battle-scenes. (Printed folio 146.)

ch03.anchor: according to the Onna Taikōki
ch03.note: The narrator's sources for the bath-house legend are pointedly modern: a 1950s newspaper serial (the Onna Taikōki) by an editor of the Yomiuri Shimbun, and the war-bombed temple’s present street address. The fabulous tale of Hideyoshi’s escape is set beside a checkable modern record — surface against underside again. (Printed folio 147.)

ch03.anchor: An uprising of the Ōmi packhorse-men
ch03.note: The bashaku were the packhorse-transport guilds of the medieval highroads, notorious for the armed risings (ikki) they mounted when tolls or prices moved against them; hence the townsfolk’s first guess at the tumult. (Printed folio 138.)

ch03.anchor: This is the seat of the Chigachi
ch03.note: The Iga Hattori line kept two seats and two surnames — Hattori at the Hattori village north of Ueno, Chigachi at Yono — a real duality preserved in the records (Hattori Hanzō is documented as Chigachi Hanzō Taira no Masashige). The narrator sets it beside, but distinguishes it from, the ninja secret of Chapter 2, where Momochi Sandayū and Fujibayashi Nagato proved to be one man. (Printed folio 153.)

ch03.anchor: At the time of the Ōnin War
ch03.note: The Ōnin War (1467–1477), a decade of civil war centered on Kyoto that gutted the authority of the Ashikaga shogunate and opened the Warring-States age. (Printed folio 154.)

ch03.anchor: through Yagyū to Nara
ch03.note: Yagyū, a village in the hills east of Nara, gave its name to the Yagyū Shinkage-ryū school of swordsmanship, whose masters became the Tokugawa house sword-instructors. (Printed folio 153.)

ch03.anchor: they call it the sanmai
ch03.note: The ryōbosei, or dual-grave custom: a corpse-burial field (the sanmai) kept apart from the site of the family gravestones. The carrying and burying of the dead, like the working of hides, was left to the hereditary outcaste communities (the eta and hinin, forebears of the modern burakumin) — a class the author, a lifelong man of the left, writes of with deliberate sympathy here and in the story of Tamo (Chapter 1). (Printed folio 157.)

ch03.anchor: Michael Steichen's Christian Daimyō
ch03.note: Michel Steichen (1857–1929), a Belgian missionary-scholar; his Les Daimyō chrétiens (1904) is an early standard account of Japan’s Christian lords. The quotation is genuine. (Printed folio 158.)

ch03.anchor: one of the Five Commissioners
ch03.note: Asano Nagamasa (1547–1611), Hideyoshi’s brother-in-law by marriage and, in time, one of the go-bugyō — the five commissioners Hideyoshi set over the day-to-day government of the realm. (Printed folio 158.)

ch03.anchor: set in order, for their very sake
ch03.note: The social charge of Lourenço’s sermon is the author’s real subject: the Christian mission reaching Japan’s poor and outcaste as a doctrine of equality before God and of a universe made for them. He treats it, as he treats Buddhism in Chapter 2’s meditation on death and rebirth, historically and materially rather than devoutly. (Printed folio 160.)

ch03.anchor: the Americanizing since the Second World War
ch03.note: One of the narrator’s fourth-wall intrusions, writing in 1962–63: he traces a Japanese susceptibility to imported culture from the Chinese continental model, through the Nanban and the Meiji “civilization and enlightenment,” to the postwar American influence he plainly resents. Murayama was twice jailed under the wartime state; his century’s grievances show through. (Printed folio 162.)

ch03.anchor: hardening that inward wish into a stone
ch03.note: The author’s materialist theory of religion, offered as his own analysis and not the source’s piety: the faith of an oppressed people (the Israelites under Rome) hardening a longing for deliverance in the next world into a creed. It is the same lens he turns on Buddhism, and on Hanzō’s and Goemon’s own unbelief. (Printed folio 168.)

ch03.anchor: no such commandments of absolute nonresistance
ch03.note: The narrator’s claim — his interpretation, not an established fact — that the Jesuit mission in Japan played down the ethic of nonresistance (“love your enemies,” “turn the other cheek”) before a clientele of warriors, so that the one commandment Hanzō found irksome was the duty of confession. (Printed folio 168.)

ch03.anchor: the Twist, or the tamure
ch03.note: Dance crazes of the narrator’s own moment, around 1962; the anachronism is his joke. The reading of the second word (タムレ) is uncertain on the scan. (Printed folio 169.)

ch03.anchor: opened a council at Kiyosu castle
ch03.note: The Kiyosu Conference of 1582, at which Nobunaga’s surviving generals settled the succession on his infant grandson Sanbōshi (later Oda Hidenobu). Hideyoshi’s manoeuvre here — backing the legitimate line against Shibata Katsuie’s candidate — set him at the head of the Oda house and on the road to the realm. (Printed folio 177.)

ch03.anchor: the Five Constant Virtues
ch03.note: The gojō, the five cardinal virtues of Confucian ethics: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith. (Printed folio 178.)

ch03.anchor: the famous seventeen-day rite at the Daitoku-ji
ch03.note: Hideyoshi’s vast funeral for Nobunaga at the Daitoku-ji in Murasakino, Kyoto, in the tenth month of 1582 — less an obsequy than a claim to the succession. He founded the Sōken-in there as Nobunaga’s mortuary temple; it still stands. (Printed folio 179.)

ch03.anchor: boiled alive in the cauldron
ch03.note: The novel’s title-motif and its destination. The legendary Ishikawa Goemon was executed by boiling (kamairi) in 1594, by tradition in an iron cauldron on the dry bed of the Kamo at Sanjō, in Kyoto — the death the whole book is moving toward, and which the narrator here lets fall thirteen years early. (Printed folio 181.)

ch03.anchor: the art of ten-ton
ch03.note: Tenton no jutsu, the ninja’s “heaven-hiding” art: the use of the sky and weather — cloud crossing the moon, wind, rain, snow — to dazzle a watcher and slip his eye. (Printed folio 182.)

ch03.anchor: a Buddha-image was carved from aloeswood
ch03.note: Nobunaga’s body was never recovered from the burning Honnō-ji; his funeral therefore had no bones to inter, and an image of scented aloeswood stood in the coffin — a fact the novel turns to account, for Goemon, who dealt the death-blow (Chapter 2), knows exactly why the coffin is empty. The Koretō Taiji-ki cited here is a contemporary record of Hideyoshi’s defeat of “Koretō” (the court title of Akechi) Mitsuhide. (Printed folio 184.)

ch03.anchor: that bald rat could never find himself a wife to match you
ch03.note: A genuine surviving letter of Nobunaga to Nene, Hideyoshi’s wife (later honored as the Kōdai-in), teasing “the bald rat” and telling her not to be jealous. “Tōkichirō” is Hideyoshi’s early name. Nobunaga’s nicknames for him — Monkey, bald rat — are both on record. (Printed folio 185.)

ch03.anchor: Namiki Gohei wrote
ch03.note: The kabuki Sanmon Gosan no Kiri — originally a scene of Namiki Gohei’s Kinmon Gosan no Kiri (Osaka, 1778) — whose gate-top tableau, with Goemon’s cry “Zekkei kana!” (“What a view!”), is among the most famous in the repertoire. It invents the meeting of Goemon and Hideyoshi at the Nanzen-ji gate (see Chapter 2, the Goemon legend of that gate). (Printed folio 192.)

ch03.anchor: the seed of thieves in the world shall never run dry
ch03.note: The couplet the play sets between the two men is the death-poem (jisei) traditionally given to Goemon: Ishikawa ya / hama no masago wa / tsukuru to mo / yo ni nusubito no / tane wa tsukumaji — “Ishikawa: though the sands of the beach be spent, the seed of thieves in the world shall never run dry.” (Printed folio 195.)

ch03.anchor: the keyhole of the great bronze door that Spain had made him a gift of
ch03.note: The narrator plants the meeting the whole novel drives at: thirteen years on, Goemon taken in an attempt on Hideyoshi’s life in the inmost chamber of his castle, glimpsed through a keyhole, and boiled for it — the “first” meeting for Hideyoshi being also the last. (Printed folio 196.)

ch03.anchor: stormed and destroyed Azai Nagamasa at Odani castle
ch03.note: Azai Nagamasa, Nobunaga’s brother-in-law turned enemy, destroyed by the Oda in 1573. His widow was Nobunaga’s sister Oichi; the daughter named here as the Lady Yodo is Chacha, who would become Hideyoshi’s consort and the mother of his heir Hideyori. Married now to Shibata Katsuie, Oichi will die with him within the year. (Printed folio 197.)

ch03.anchor: it was here that Hideyoshi's army and Mitsuhide's had fought
ch03.note: The Battle of Yamazaki (2 July 1582 in the old calendar), where Hideyoshi crushed Mitsuhide eleven days after the Honnō-ji, avenging Nobunaga and clearing his own path. The struggle for the height of Mount Tennō gave Japanese the proverb tennōzan for the decisive turning-point of any contest. (Printed folio 198.)

ch04.note: The chapter's title, Ikusa ikusa — literally 'war, war' — names the stretch it covers: the Shizugatake campaign and the fall of the house of Shibata, one war treading on the heels of the last. (Printed folio 199.)

A shimenawa is a rope of twisted rice-straw hung with paper streamers, marking off sacred or purified ground; at the New Year one is strung over a doorway to keep the coming year's ill luck out. (Printed folio 200.)
'Bald rat' (hage-nezumi) was Nobunaga's own scornful pet name for Hideyoshi, known from a surviving letter of his; here Goemon borrows it. (Printed folio 201.)

ch04.anchor: Reckonings and loincloths both slip loose from the far end.
ch04.note: A rustic proverb: atekoto to fundoshi wa mukō kara hazureru, 'reckonings and loincloths both come loose from the far side' — what you count on fails of its own accord, and from the direction you least expect. (Printed folio 202.)

A charm muttered to turn away lightning and misfortune. By one tradition the lands (kuwabara, mulberry-field) of a former Sugawara estate were never struck, the thunder-god sparing his own old ground. (Printed folio 202.)

The old lunisolar calendar kept step with the sun by inserting a thirteenth 'leap' month as needed; Tenshō 11 carried a second, intercalary first month, so the year held two New Years. (Printed folio 203.)
A gohei is a ritual wand hung with zigzag paper streamers, used in Shinto to summon or embody a god; Katsuie bore its shape worked in gold as his field standard (umajirushi). (Printed folio 205.)
Hachiman, god of war, was worshipped in syncretic form as a bodhisattva (daibosatsu); his name on a war-banner was held to overawe the enemy. (Printed folio 206.)

ch04.anchor: He had his Iga ration pills by him
ch04.note: The shinobi's hyōrōgan: a compound of dried rice, buckwheat, bonito, dried loach, pickled-plum flesh and steamed pine-bark, rolled into pills said to sustain a man ten days. The recipe that follows is given in momme (about 3.75 grams) and bu (about 3 millimeters). (Printed folio 221.)

The young spearmen decorated for valor at Shizugatake — among them Katō Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori — became a fixture of popular history and the stage. As the author notes, nine men were in fact commended; 'seven' was chosen for its ring. (Printed folio 220.)

ch04.anchor: faced a raging tiger with a cross-bladed spear
ch04.note: Katō Kiyomasa's tiger-hunt in the mountains of Korea, with a cross-bladed spear (jūmonji-yari), is among the best-loved episodes of his legend. (Printed folio 220.)

Hideyoshi's celebrated 'Great Return' (ō-gaeshi): on word of the raid he raced some fifty kilometers by night from Ōgaki back to the Shizugatake front, feeding and lighting the road from the villages, and struck before Katsuie's army could turn its success to account. (Printed folio 225.)
Hideyoshi's famous sen-nari byōtan, the 'thousand-gourd' standard: by legend a gourd was added for each victory until the pole bore a golden cluster of them. (Printed folio 227.)

ch04.anchor: in a letter he sent on the eighteenth of December
ch04.note: Luís Fróis (see Chapter 1), the mission's chronicler, described Shizugatake in a genuine dispatch to the Visitor Valignano; Murayama quotes it, then adds — with a wink — that its only possible witness at the castle's heart was Goemon. (Printed folio 237.)

Three stock exemplars of the retainer who dies in his lord's place: Ji Xin, who impersonated Liu Bang so the Han founder could escape Xiang Yu; Satō Tadanobu, who covered Yoshitsune's flight; and Murakami Yoshiteru (Hikoshirō), who died in Prince Morinaga's stead. (Printed folio 239.)

ch04.anchor: famed from her girlhood as the fairest in the realm
ch04.note: Oichi (see Chapter 3), Nobunaga's sister and one of the noted beauties of the age. The portrait the author describes, commissioned by her daughter Yodogimi (the Lady Yodo), survives at the Jimyō-in on Mount Kōya. (Printed folio 246.)
Katsuie's tower at Kita-no-shō was among the first of the great multi-storied keeps, said to rise nine tiers; it burned with him and his household. (Printed folio 243.)
The aristocratic hikimayu: the natural brows were shaved and two lozenge- or moth-shaped brows painted high on the forehead, a court fashion of the age. (Printed folio 248.)

ch04.anchor: a death worse even than crucifixion
ch04.note: Azai Manpukumaru, Oichi's son and the Azai heir, was hunted out after Odani fell in 1573 and put to death by impalement at Kinomoto; the deed is laid variously to Nobunaga's order and, as here, to Hideyoshi's hand. (Printed folio 253.)
The source gives Oichi's age as thirty-seven on folio 246 and thirty-six here; both are rendered as printed. (Printed folio 255.)

ch05.anchor: followed their lord into death
ch05.note: The custom of junshi, in which retainers took their own lives to follow a dead lord, so as not to survive him. It was still admired in the sixteenth century; the Tokugawa shogunate would later forbid it as a waste of good men. (Printed folio 258.)

ch05.anchor: The realm of the Asura, he thought
ch05.note: The ashura (Sanskrit asura) are the demigods of the Buddhist cosmos, ruled by wrath and consumed in ceaseless war; the “realm of the Asura” is one of the six paths of rebirth, a world of unending strife. Goemon means: this battlefield is that hell, and every man on it a demon of it. (Printed folio 259.)

ch05.anchor: the Doll's Festival
ch05.note: The Hina-matsuri, kept on the third day of the third month, when families with daughters set out a tiered display of court dolls. To arrive with a grilled eel rather than the season's sweets is part of Hatsuko’s comic bluntness. (Printed folio 261.)

ch05.anchor: love between men was a common thing
ch05.note: Male love (nanshoku) was indeed openly accepted among the warrior class of the age, between an older samurai and a youth; the narrator’s point is that female homoeroticism, by contrast, went unrecorded and unremarked. The frankness is the author’s own. (Printed folio 262.)

ch05.anchor: made it into chagayu
ch05.note: Chagayu, “tea-gruel,” is rice boiled thin in water steeped with a bag of tea leaves and seasoned with salt—a way of stretching a little rice across many meals. It was a daily staple of the poor of the Kii and Yamato hill country, where rice was scarce. (Printed folio 263.)

ch05.anchor: The Kakuban of Maki's song
ch05.note: Kakuban (1095–1143), an eminent monk of Mount Kōya who quarreled with its scholar-monks and founded the reformed Shingi Shingon school; the Negoro-ji became its center. Maki’s lullaby names him and the hill above the temple. The song’s word tojiyori is genuinely obscure, as the narrator says. (Printed folio 270.)

ch05.anchor: before Fudō Myōō
ch05.note: Fudō Myōō (Sanskrit Acala), the “Immovable” wisdom-king, is shown wreathed in flame, sword in hand, his fierce look meant to burn away delusion. The goma is the esoteric fire-rite performed before him, in which sticks are burned to signify the consuming of earthly passion. (Printed folio 266.)

ch05.anchor: the art of war of Sun Tzu
ch05.note: The Sunzi bingfa, the classic of strategy ascribed to Sun Wu of ancient China (c. 5th century B.C.), the oldest and most famous of military treatises. The author’s claim that En no Gyōja put it to use is legend, not history. (Printed folio 266.)

ch05.anchor: the outcasts of their day
ch05.note: The wandering hijiri of Kōya, mendicant holy men who lived apart in the mountain valleys, were reckoned outside the settled order and lumped with the hinin, the “non-persons” of the outcast class. The author, a man of the political left, dwells on their oppression and on the faith that was their one refuge. (Printed folio 268.)

ch05.anchor: the Thirty-three Places of the Western Country
ch05.note: The Saikoku Sanjūsankasho, a circuit of thirty-three temples of Kannon across the provinces west of the capital; pilgrims sang a set hymn (goeika) at each. The Kokawa-dera is the third station. (Printed folio 271.)

ch05.anchor: Chikuzen-dono has built here
ch05.note: “Lord Chikuzen” is Hideyoshi, from his court title Hashiba Chikuzen-no-kami; the Jesuit letter-writers commonly name him so. Frōis measures Osaka against Nobunaga’s castle at Azuchi, which he had also seen. (Printed folio 280.)

ch05.anchor: more than one legua
ch05.note: A legua is the Portuguese league; a cruzado a Portuguese gold coin. The author supplies the conversions Frōis’s readers lacked: a league at about 5.6 kilometers, a cruzado at ten monme of silver. (Printed folio 281.)

ch05.anchor: Tsuboi Sakae's Twenty-Four Eyes
ch05.note: Nijūshi no Hitomi (1952), a much-loved novel by Tsuboi Sakae set on Shōdoshima, following a village teacher and her twelve pupils through the militarist years and the war; a famous film was made of it in 1954. The author cites it as a fellow writer would. (Printed folio 283.)

ch05.anchor: put in at Tanegashima
ch05.note: The traditional date for the coming of the matchlock to Japan: in 1543 a Portuguese ship reached the island of Tanegashima off southern Kyūshū, and its lord bought two guns from a merchant aboard. The account the narrator quotes, the Teppd-ki, was written some sixty years later by the monk Nanpō Bunshi. (Printed folio 285.)

ch05.anchor: at the time of the Seinan War
ch05.note: The Seinan War, or Satsuma Rebellion, of 1877 (Meiji 10): the last great samurai revolt, led by Saigō Takamori against the new imperial government. Three hundred and thirty-five years after 1543 places the guns’ destruction in that year. (Printed folio 286.)

ch05.anchor: gave his own daughter Wakasa
ch05.note: The legend of the screw-breech: to learn how the barrel was plugged at its base, the smith Yasaka Kinbei is said to have given his daughter Wakasa to the foreign captain. The author, telling it plainly, lets its cost stand: to learn a screw-thread, a man gave up a daughter. (Printed folio 288.)

ch05.anchor: Forty-two is a man's great unlucky year
ch05.note: In Japanese reckoning certain ages are yakudoshi, years of ill fortune, the gravest for a man being forty-two; the years before and after are the lesser maeyaku and atoyaku. Ieyasu counts his flight through Iga (at forty-one) as the first, and the coming war with Hideyoshi (at forty-three) as the last. “The rent falls due” renders an idiom for one’s time being up. (Printed folio 290.)

ch05.anchor: raised Nobukatsu as his brocade banner
ch05.note: The nishiki no mihata, the brocade standard, was properly the imperial banner that marked the legitimate side in war; here it is figurative. By fighting in the name of Nobunaga’s surviving son, Ieyasu gave his cause a show of legitimacy against Hideyoshi. (Printed folio 290.)

ch05.anchor: The Komaki-Nagakute campaign now to come
ch05.note: The campaign of Tenshō 12 (1584) between Hideyoshi and the allied Ieyasu and Oda Nobukatsu, named for the standoff at Mount Komaki and the battle at Nagakute. It ended in no clear military decision but in a settlement that left Ieyasu’s standing raised, as the narrator goes on to show. (Printed folio 292.)

ch05.anchor: a retainer named Kani Saizō happened by
ch05.note: Kani Saizō (Kani Yoshinaga) was a warrior famous enough that his brusque refusal here—his one horse being “an umbrella in a downpour,” a thing there is no lending when it is needed most—became a remembered anecdote. (Printed folio 311.)

ch05.anchor: took the name Hashiba Hideyasu
ch05.note: Ieyasu’s second son, sent to Hideyoshi as an adopted son and hostage: called Ogimaru as a boy, then Hashiba Hideyasu, and later known to history as Yūki Hideyasu (1574–1607). The court rank and the ten thousand koku were the honors of the adoption. (Printed folio 346.)

ch05.anchor: a nun by the name of Kiara
ch05.note: “Kiara” is the Christian baptismal name Clara. This is Tamo, the woman ninja of the earlier chapters: sent into the Asakura castle at Ichijōdani, burned when Nobunaga fell on Iga (shielded by her lover Kashii), and afterward the ruined beggar of the novel’s opening. That the oppressed found in the foreign faith their one comfort is the author’s recurring theme. (Printed folio 333.)

ch05.anchor: The old badger has not laid eyes on Hatsuko
ch05.note: “The old badger” (tanuki-jiji) is Hanzō’s scornful name for Ieyasu; the tanuki, a badger-like animal of folklore, stands for a sly and dissembling old schemer, and the epithet clung to Ieyasu ever after. (Printed folio 339.)

ch05.anchor: his own mother killed at his order
ch05.note: Hanzō’s charge in his rage. Ieyasu did in fact force his eldest son, Nobuyasu, to take his own life in 1579, and his first wife with him; but his mother, Odai-no-kata, outlived him. The exaggeration is the measure of Hanzō’s bitterness, and is rendered here as printed. (Printed folio 331.)

ch06.note: Kudoyama (Kūdoyama), on the Kino River below Mount Kōya, is where Sanada Yukimura (Nobushige, 1567–1615) settled in exile after Sekigahara, and from which he rode to the defense of Osaka Castle, dying in its fall. Sarutobi Sasuke and Kirigakure Saizō are the best known of his legendary “Ten Braves,” ninja heroes of later popular fiction rather than of history. The Sanada Ninja Band (真田忍者群, Sanada ninja-gun) is the author’s own sequel to this novel. (Printed folio 360.)

The Retired Emperor Shirakawa (1053–1129), who ruled for decades from behind the throne as a cloistered sovereign, is traditionally said to have named three things beyond even his command: the floodwaters of the Kamo River, the fall of the dice, and the warrior-monks of Mount Hiei. The saying is recorded in the Genpei Seisuiki and elsewhere; corroborated as a long-standing attribution, though, like most such sayings, it cannot be traced to his own mouth. (Printed folio 364.)

ch06.anchor: not in Goemon's age only, but down to the present day
ch06.note: The Great Pagoda (Daitō) of the Negoro-ji is a real building and survives to this day: a two-storied tahōtō some forty meters high, the largest of its kind in Japan and a National Treasure. It came through Hideyoshi’s burning of the temple in 1585, and its timbers still carry the marks of musket-balls, as the author reports from his own visit. (Printed folio 368.)

ch06.anchor: the Age of the Latter Law
ch06.note: The Age of the Latter Law (mappō) is, in Buddhist reckoning, the third and final, degenerate age of the Dharma, when the teaching still stands but no one can any longer win enlightenment by it. Medieval Japan widely held that this age had begun in 1052, a belief that colored much of its religious life. (Printed folio 372.)

The sword-hunt (katanagari): Hideyoshi’s famous edict of 1588 stripped the peasantry and the temples of swords, spears, and firearms, on the pretext of melting the metal into nails and clamps for a great image of the Buddha. It disarmed the countryside and hardened the line between samurai and commoner. The Negoro confiscation of 1585 described here was an early, local forerunner. (Printed folio 382.)

ch06.anchor: to bring first Kishū, and then Shikoku, to heel
ch06.note: Historical: in the third month of Tenshō 13 (1585) Hideyoshi led a large army into Kii to break the Negoro-ji, the warrior-monks of Saiga, and the other autonomous powers of the province. The forward forts fell, the Negoro-ji was stormed and burned on the twenty-third, and the campaign went on to reduce the whole peninsula; Shikoku was invaded that summer. The novel’s account follows the recorded course of the war. (Printed folio 380.)

ch06.anchor: the very homeland of Dainichi Nyorai
ch06.note: Dainichi Nyorai (Sanskrit Mahāvairocana), the cosmic “Great Sun” Buddha, is the central object of worship of the Shingon school, of whom all other Buddhas — and the wisdom-king Fudō Myōō, met earlier — are held to be emanations. To call Negoro the homeland of Dainichi is to claim the temple as sacred Shingon ground. (Printed folio 384.)

The Water Margin (Chinese Shuihu zhuan, Japanese Suikoden) is one of the great vernacular novels of Ming China, a sprawling tale of a band of a hundred and eight outlaws. Hugely popular in Edo Japan, it shaped much of its heroic and historical fiction; the author’s point is that the Shinsho Taikōki is embroidered romance of that stamp, not sober record. (Printed folio 409.)

ch06.anchor: slapping the desk with their paper fans
ch06.note: Kōshaku was the professional art of reciting war-tales and histories from a raised seat to a paying audience, the reciter marking his cadences by rapping a folding fan (the hariōgi) on his small desk. Its stock-in-trade was just this kind of heroic battle-chronicle; the author sets its rousing theater against the squalor of the real killing. (Printed folio 411.)
